rashi:a1.1: It might enter your mind to say: granted at the outset [before the lottery], we require unblemished animals, because I do not know whether this one will be fixed for the Name or that one will be fixed for the Name, etc.
rashi:a1.2: Another version [of the discussion at the end of 6b]: “But the lottery fixes only…” Rav Yosef said: Whose view is this? It is Ḥanan the Egyptian, who does not require a lottery, as it is taught: Ḥanan the Egyptian says: Even if the blood of the goat offered inside is in the cup and [the scapegoat] died, that is, [the inner goat] was already slaughtered and the scapegoat died, he brings its fellow: he brings another goat from the market, pairs it with it and stands it beside the blood, to show that it is its fellow, and afterward sends it away. Evidently he does not require a lottery, and the challenge we raised cannot be raised; therefore the verse was needed.
rashi:a1.3: And he challenges: Say that you heard of Ḥanan that he does not hold of deferral, that is, that one does not bring two other goats, draw lots, slaughter one for the Name and send the other to Azazel, while the first, already slaughtered, is deferred and its blood poured out to waste. But did you hear from him that he does not hold of a lottery? Perhaps he actually brings two from the market and draws lots; the one on which the lot for Azazel falls is stood beside the blood in the cup and sent away, the blood in the cup is sprinkled according to its law, and the one on which the lot for the Name fell grazes until it becomes blemished. Rather, whose view is it, that requires a verse to include the goat so that it may not be blemished? It is Rabbi Shimon, who does not hold of a lottery. This is the conclusion, and nothing further is challenged. The reading “Say that you heard of Rabbi Shimon, etc.” is an error, for in tractate Yoma (63b), in the chapter Shnei Se’irei, we learn this whole discussion and nothing is challenged there.
rashi:a1.4: Rava said: For example, where it became blemished, etc.: as I explained above, this is part of the first [answer]. The answer that reads “for example, where he had a sick person in his house, etc.” we do not read here; it is an error, for here the discussion does not deal with an animal lacking time at all. But in tractate Yoma (ibid.) we learn it in that discussion, where there is a contradiction concerning an animal lacking time. Here one cannot say “if it is not needed for a blemished animal, apply it to one lacking time,” for we derive lacking time for the scapegoat from “unto the Lord” of the other verse, “and from the eighth day onward”; it is from here that it is derived in tractate Yoma (63b).
gershom:a1.1: The Master said: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, says: also for the collection of the blood, etc. [According to the first tanna,] “upon the altar” is the manner of the verse to speak thus and does not come for exposition; rather, “you shall not offer” comes [for sprinkling].
gershom:a2.1: And for Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, too, it is the manner of the verse and does not come for exposition, and this “you shall not offer” is needed for the sprinkling of the blood.
tosafot:a4.1: “And from the hand of a foreigner you shall not offer… of any of these”: And if you ask: why do I need “any man” to include descendants of Noah, who vow vows and gift offerings like Israel (Ḥullin 13b)? Derive it from this verse, for since it says “you shall not offer these,” it implies: these you do not offer, but you do offer unblemished ones. The reverse question does not arise, why do I need “from the hand of a foreigner” when it could be derived from “any man,” since “foreigner” is needed for the exposition here: whether on their altar or on our altar. Rather, why do I need “any man”? Rabbeinu Shimshon bar Avraham answered that it is needed for the dispute of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva in the chapter Ve’elu Menaḥot (Menaḥot 73b): What does the verse teach by “for a burnt offering”? To exclude nazirite offerings; Rabbi Akiva says: “burnt offering”: I have only a burnt offering, not other offerings.
gershom:a3.1: But collection of the blood, from where does he derive it? He derives it from this: “And from the hand of a foreigner you shall not offer.” The descendants of Noah were commanded only regarding animals lacking limbs, as it is written: “Of every living thing of all flesh” (Genesis 6:19): bring an animal whose principal limbs are alive.
rashi:a5.1: The descendants of Noah were commanded not to sacrifice animals lacking limbs, as we say in the first chapter of Avoda Zara (5b), but regarding any other blemish they were not commanded, on their own altar. And had it not been written “neither from the hand of a foreigner shall you offer… of any of these,” which implies that a blemished animal is not accepted from a gentile to be sacrificed, I would have said it may be offered, provided only that it is not lacking a limb. It teaches us [otherwise].
gershom:a4.1: It might enter your mind: on our altar it should be permitted to bring their offering that is blemished, but not lacking a limb.
rashi:a5.2: On their bama: on a private altar that the gentile made to Heaven. And it teaches us by “of any of these” that we do not accept: that is, this is why we do not accept it, since it is written in that verse “of any of these,” implying you shall not accept a blemished animal; so too for them, on the designated altar [in the Temple].
gershom:a5.1: It teaches us: “Neither from the hand of a foreigner shall you offer… there is a blemish in them”: [any] permanent blemish.
gershom:a6.1: [It excludes a private altar: it is prohibited to sacrifice a blemished animal on it.]
gershom:a7.1: We too should accept from them: to sacrifice their offering on our altar, blemished with a permanent blemish that is not a missing limb.
gershom:a8.1: It teaches us “of any of these,” like us: just as for us, [blemishes] like bruised and crushed, which are not a missing limb but a permanent blemish, we do not sacrifice, so too from them we shall not accept.
rashi:a10.1: Reish Lakish objects: he is referring back to the statement above that one transgresses five prohibitions. Perhaps we learned that one is flogged for “you shall not consecrate” only with an unblemished animal that became blemished, for one can say: since it was unblemished at the outset, he thought, “Even though a blemish befell it, I will consecrate it and sacrifice it,” and since we can say he had sacrifice in mind when he consecrated it, he is flogged. But an animal blemished from the outset, from its mother’s womb, is a mere date palm, for one can say he did not have in mind that it was fit to be sacrificed but consecrated it only for its value, and he is not flogged.
tosafot:a10.1: Only with an unblemished animal that became blemished: for one can say that since it was unblemished at the outset, he thought, “Even though a blemish befell it, I will consecrate it and sacrifice it,” and since we can say he had sacrifice in mind when he consecrated it, he is flogged; but an animal blemished from the outset, from its mother’s womb, is a mere date palm, and one can say he did not have in mind that it was fit to be sacrificed. This is Rashi’s wording. Our teacher [the text reads הר״ר מר] found it difficult: how can we say he did not have sacrifice in mind, when they warned him, “Do not offer a blemished animal for the altar,” and he accepted the warning and said, “On that condition I am doing it”? Without that he is not flogged. Therefore the Maharam thought to explain that Reish Lakish refers not to “you shall not consecrate” but to “you shall not burn” and “you shall not sprinkle,” and this is the meaning: they taught that he transgresses “you shall not burn” and “you shall not sprinkle” only when he consecrated it unblemished and it became blemished, for since the sanctity of the altar took hold of it before it became blemished, he has in mind that it is fit to be sacrificed. But one blemished from the outset, before its consecration, is a mere date palm; he does not have in mind that it is fit to be sacrificed, and he is not flogged.
gershom:a9.1: Reish Lakish objects: Perhaps we learned only, etc. He refers to the baraita that teaches: “From here they said: one who consecrates blemished animals for the altar transgresses five prohibitions.” And he says: perhaps we learned that one is flogged only for an animal that was unblemished at the outset and became blemished, and not for every blemished animal; for one that is blemished from the outset, why is he flogged? It is a mere date palm; let it be as though he consecrated a mere date palm for the altar, which is saying nothing, since it was never fit for the altar. And why does [the baraita] teach “blemished” without qualification, which implies also one blemished from the outset?
rashi:a11.1: Saru’a [too long]: one of whose limbs was broken [so the printed text; Rabbeinu Gershom, below, explains saru’a as one whose thigh is extended].
rashi:a11.2: Kalut [too short]: whose hooves are uncloven.
rashi:a11.3: Are written in the passage: and about them it is written “you shall not offer,” which we expound as “you shall not consecrate.”
gershom:a10.1: Rav Ḥiyya bar Yosef said to him: this is why it teaches without qualification: saru’a and kalut are written in the passage of blemished animals, and these are blemished from the outset, as we said in the chapter Al Elu Mumin [Bekhorot 40b]: saru’a, whose thigh is extended; kalut, whose legs are uncloven like those of a donkey or a horse.
rashi:a12.1: Perhaps we learned only: that one is liable for consecration only with substitution, for substitution takes effect on an animal with a permanent blemish, and it is fully sacred: it does not go out to non-sacred status to be shorn and worked even through redemption, but is like other consecrated animals whose consecration preceded their blemish. This mishna is below, in the second chapter (Temurah 16b), as it is written: “good for bad or bad for good, and if he shall substitute,” etc. And since it is full sanctity, he is flogged for it if he substituted, bringing a blemished animal to consecrate and it took effect as the substitute for an unblemished consecrated animal. But if he consecrated an animal blemished from the outset, I would not say he is flogged, for it is a mere date palm, unless he sacrificed it.
gershom:a11.1: Perhaps we learned that one is flogged only with substitution, where he substituted with a blemished animal.
gershom:a12.1: As we learned: there is greater stringency with substitution than with consecrated animals, in that sanctity takes hold of an animal with a permanent blemish, as it is written: “He shall not substitute it… good for bad or bad for good”; that is a blemished animal; and it is written: “And if he shall substitute… then both it and its substitute shall be sacred.” Since sanctity takes hold of it with a permanent blemish, it does not go out to non-sacred status to be shorn and worked, which is not so with other consecrated animals: other consecrated animals whose permanent blemish preceded their consecration go out to non-sacred status to be shorn and worked. And perhaps the baraita teaches about one who consecrates a blemished animal through substitution.
rashi:a13.1: They were counted and concluded: this implies that they examined carefully and found no more. And if it were so that [the baraita] speaks of substitution,
rashi:a13.2: There would be six, for there is also the prohibition “he shall not substitute.”
rashi:a13.3: Rather, what? With an animal blemished from the outset? And through consecration, why is he flogged? The sanctity of the altar does not take hold of it at all, for it is a mere date palm, and he consecrated it only for its value.
rashi:a15.1: There is none of its kind: fit for the altar.
rashi:a15.2: A blemished animal has [something] of its kind: fit for the altar. And since there is something of its kind that is fit, there is disgrace, since he left something fit and consecrated something unfit.
gershom:a13.1: Even so, the matter is disgraceful: for one who consecrates an animal blemished from the outset [is more repugnant than one who consecrates] a date palm. One who consecrates a date palm causes no disgrace, for with a date palm there is nothing of its kind more choice than it. But an animal blemished from the outset: since there is something of its kind that is fit, and he consecrates a blemished one, he is flogged, [even if he consecrates it for the value of libations, so that libations are brought with its money, he is flogged]. [A marginal note here reads: “should read ‘in the mishna’.”] [Rather, why do I need “it”?] Since you expound “gift” and “vow” together, what does “it” come for? For that which is taught, etc.
rashi:a16.1: Even if he consecrated it for the value of libations: where there is now not so much disgrace, since nothing of its kind is fit for libations; and furthermore he consecrated it for its value. Even so, he is flogged.
tosafot:a16.1: Even if he consecrated it for the value of libations he is flogged: and the same applies to one who consecrates it for the value of a burnt offering. And as for what is said below (Temurah 18b), that one who consecrates a female for a burnt offering, it is sold and its money goes for a burnt offering, one must say that he is flogged. Likewise what we learned in the chapter Keitzad Ma’arimin (below, Temurah 27b): if he said of a non-kosher animal or of a blemished one, “These are a burnt offering,” he has said nothing; “These are for a burnt offering,” they are sold and he brings a burnt offering with their money; one must say that he is flogged.
rashi:b1.1: “You may offer it for a gift”: a blemished animal, for the value of consecrated property for Temple maintenance; for the altar it cannot be offered, as it is written: “You shall not give of them” (Leviticus 22:22), etc.
rashi:b1.2: I have only: the inclusion permitting one to consecrate a blemished animal for Temple maintenance,
rashi:b1.3: only by way of a gift, for example: “This is for Temple maintenance.”
rashi:b1.4: From where a vow: that if he said, “It is incumbent on me [to give] an animal for the value of Temple maintenance,” it is a mitzva to set aside a blemished one? The verse states: “And for a vow.” He expounds it thus: “You may offer it for a gift, and for a vow,” that is, and likewise for a vow.
rashi:b2.1: “It shall not be accepted”: these are offerings for the altar, to which acceptance applies.
rashi:b2.2: I have only a vow: since “vow” is adjacent to “it shall not be accepted,” and it implies that if he vowed, “It is incumbent on me [to bring] a burnt offering,” he may not bring a blemished animal.
rashi:b2.3: From where a gift: that he may not say of a blemished animal, “This is for the altar”?
rashi:b2.4: The verse states: “a gift… and for a vow it shall not be accepted.” It is expounded thus: “A gift that you make of it, or a vow: it shall not be accepted.”
rashi:b2.5: Rabbi says: “It shall not be accepted”: the verse speaks of the acceptance of its body, that he may not sacrifice it; this too refers to offerings for the altar, like the first tanna.
rashi:b4.1: And he asks: Rather, what does “it” come for? That is, granted, the whole verse you establish for the exposition you expounded, this “gift” and “vow”;
rashi:b4.2: but “it,” as written in “you may offer it for a gift,” why do I need it?
rashi:b4.3: It: a blemished animal you may consecrate for Temple maintenance, etc.
rashi:b4.4: Transgresses a positive mitzva: this positive mitzva, that we say “but you may not consecrate unblemished ones,” which is a prohibition derived from a positive mitzva, and it counts as a positive mitzva.
gershom:b1.1: Transgresses a positive mitzva: for a prohibition derived from a positive mitzva is a positive mitzva.
rashi:b6.1: “No” is stated in the matters: that is, in that passage.
rashi:b6.2: “No” shall you say: that is, thus the Holy One, blessed be He, said: a prohibition is said to Israel; there is a prohibition here, so that if they transgress this passage they transgress a prohibition.
rashi:b7.1: Limbs, etc.: the pieces, as is the law of a burnt offering.
gershom:b2.1: The limbs of blemished animals: the sacrificial portions. He is flogged for burning all of it and for burning part of it, since “all of it” includes “part of it.” And Abaye said: one is not flogged for a general prohibition, a prohibition that includes two prohibitions, for every burning of all of it and every burning of part of it come from one prohibition, from “you shall not give.”
rashi:b7.2: For a general prohibition: for burning all of it and part of it come from one prohibition, “nor make an offering by fire of them,” as I explained above. But for all the others there is a prohibition for each one: consecration comes from “whatever has a blemish, you shall not offer,” which we expounded above (Temurah 6b) as “you shall not consecrate”; slaughter from “you shall not offer these unto the Lord,” said of the blind or broken; and sprinkling from “you shall not offer” said of the bruised or crushed [Leviticus 22:24]. The “one is not flogged” that Abaye said means one is not flogged twice, but once one is, according to the one who says that for a general prohibition one is at least flogged once, at the end of the second chapter of Pesaḥim (41b).
tosafot:b7.1: Abaye said: one is not flogged for a general prohibition: Rashi explained that the “one is not flogged” that Abaye said means one is not flogged twice, but once one is, according to the one who says that for a general prohibition one is at least flogged once, at the end of the chapter Kol Sha’a (Pesaḥim 41b). This is Rashi’s wording, and so the discussion proves.
rashi:b8.1: For five prohibitions: and it counts these two as two.
rashi:b9.1: It teaches about men: we are not dealing with a case where, if one person did both, he is flogged twice; rather it teaches each matter separately: if he burned all of it he transgresses “you shall not burn all of it,” or if one person burns part of it he is flogged for “part of it.” But if one person does both, he is flogged only for “all of it.”
gershom:b3.1: It teaches about men: if there are five, one consecrates, one slaughters and one burns, each one is flogged.
rashi:b10.1: Remove one of them, either “all of it” or “part of it,” and insert collection of the blood, which comes from “you shall not offer” in “neither from the hand of a foreigner.”
rashi:b10.2: And he challenges: the first tanna does not hold of collection of the blood, yet he counts five.
rashi:b11.1: The first clause is the Rabbis: that is, the first clause follows the Rabbis, who do not hold one liable for collection of the blood, and even so it counts five; and this is difficult for Abaye.
rashi:b12.1: Mishna. The priests substitute for their own: offerings that a priest set aside for himself; if he substituted for them, the substitutes are caught up [in sanctity].
gershom:b4.1: Mishna. The priests substitute for their own offerings, and Israelites substitute for their own.
rashi:b12.2: Neither for a sin offering nor for a guilt offering: that an Israelite gave him to sacrifice on his behalf. If the priest substituted for it, he does not effect a substitute through it, since he has no share in it until the sacrificial portions have been burned, when he acquires the meat. And a baraita in this chapter says: a person cannot consecrate something that is not his.
rashi:b12.3: Nor for a firstborn: that an Israelite gave him; the reason is explained here in the mishna itself.
rashi:b12.4: For what reason can priests not substitute for a firstborn? Isn’t it entirely theirs? [The Israelite] gives it to him while it is alive, and the Israelite does not achieve atonement through it.
rashi:b12.5: Just as priests do not substitute for a sin offering and a guilt offering: for it is certainly obvious to us that he acquires them only once the sacrificial portions have been burned.
gershom:b5.1: Priests do not substitute for the sin offering or the guilt offering of an Israelite.
rashi:b13.1: What is it to me if he does not substitute for a sin offering and a guilt offering: that is, it is logical that priests do not substitute for a sin offering and a guilt offering, etc.
tosafot:b13.1: Which they do not acquire during their lifetimes: And if you ask: even if they did acquire them during their lifetimes, how could they substitute, according to the one in the Gemara who says that we follow the one who achieves atonement? One can answer that he means [we follow] the one who achieves atonement as well, and does not come to exclude the owners.
rashi:b13.2: It and its substitute: it juxtaposes the substitute to the consecrated animal itself. Where does sanctity take hold of the consecrated animal? In the owner’s house. So too a substitute takes effect only in the owner’s house; in the priest’s house it does not fully take effect. Therefore a priest does not substitute for a firstborn, but an Israelite, if he substituted for it, it is caught up in sanctity, for the sanctity of the firstborn took hold in his domain.
gershom:b6.1: “Then both it and its substitute shall be sacred”: that is, the sanctity of the substituted animal took hold of it in the owner’s house; so too every substitution is in the owner’s house. Once it has come into the priest’s hand it has left the owner’s house; therefore they do not substitute.
rashi:b14.1: Gemara. They sell it unblemished and alive: as it stands this implies both when the Temple stands and in the present, and it means: if the Temple stands, they sell it alive from priest to priest, and that priest sacrifices it; but slaughtered, no, for that is a disgrace to consecrated items, as it is not proper to trade in something from which part is offered on the altar. And if in the present, they sell it unblemished and alive, whether from priest to priest or from priest to Israelite, and the buyer waits until a blemish befalls it and eats it. For a firstborn in the present, once a blemish befalls it, carries only the prohibition of robbery, of robbing the priest; if a priest sold it or gave it to him, it is permitted to eat it, as we say in Bekhorot, chapter Kol Pesulei HaMukdashin (32b), regarding a blemished firstborn: Beit Hillel permit, and even a gentile may eat of it. But an unblemished slaughtered one does not exist in the present.
rashi:b14.2: And one betroths with it: a priest betroths a woman with it, for it is his property.
gershom:b7.1: Gemara. A firstborn, they sell it: the priests, unblemished and alive, and blemished, alive or slaughtered; and one betroths a woman with it, for it is their property.
rashi:b14.3: They taught only: that a priest can sell it alive
rashi:b14.4: only in the present: when it does not stand for sacrifice,
rashi:b14.5: and the priest has acquisition in it: during its lifetime, for in the present too firstborns belong to the priests.
rashi:b14.6: They do not sell it unblemished and alive: for the priest acquires it only once the sacrificial portions have been burned.
tosafot:b14.1: They taught this only in the present: And if you ask: in the chapter Shor SheNagaḥ et HaPara (Bava Kamma 53b), regarding “an ox and an ox of disqualified consecrated animals that gored,” Abaye said half damages and established it with a forewarned ox, but an ox of disqualified consecrated animals [that gored] is exempt; evidently “his fellow’s” does not apply to it. And it says there too that an ordinary person’s ox that gored an ox of disqualified consecrated animals is liable, implying that “his fellow’s” does apply. One must say that the first case speaks of a firstborn, which cannot be redeemed, and the baraita of other consecrated animals, which are redeemed on account of their blemish. And there it speaks of the present, for the Amoraim discussing it there did not live in Temple times, and even so it says there that it is not his property. If so, it is difficult, since here it says that in the present it is his property. One must say that here follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and there follows the Rabbis. And although in the first chapter of Bava Kamma (12b) it says [let him answer:] this follows Rabbi Yosei and this the Rabbis, one must say that according to this, that discussion in the chapter HaPara cannot be explained this way.
gershom:b8.1: Since the priest has acquisition in it: for since there is no altar, it is entirely the priest’s.
rashi:b15.1: Is there an unblemished slaughtered one? That would be a consecrated animal [slaughtered] outside [the Temple].
gershom:b9.1: If in the present, is there an unblemished slaughtered one? But one does not slaughter a firstborn in the present except on account of its blemish, as we learned in Bekhorot: “It happened with an old male ram,” etc.
rashi:b16.1: Does it teach “slaughtered, no”: which would imply that it is not in the present, since in the present there is no unblemished slaughtered one?
rashi:b16.2: It comes to teach us this itself: that is, what is taught [in the mishna] itself was needed to teach us that they sell it unblemished and alive, since it might enter your mind that they have no acquisition in them until a blemish befalls it; it is not so that you should infer from it “slaughtered, no,” for it deals with the present, and in the present there is no unblemished slaughtered one.
gershom:b10.1: No, actually in the present. As for your difficulty, “Is there an unblemished slaughtered one?”: does it teach explicitly, “but unblemished and slaughtered, no”? It does not teach that; rather it teaches us this itself: that they sell it unblemished and alive, and in the present.
